flag, byte range, row/column\n  points, and `is_error`, `has_error`, `is_missing`, `is_extra` flags.\n- `verify_full_match()` for reporting error and missing links in a selected\n  source region.\n- token\n  links ordered by source span.\n- `projected_links()` for viewing the same lossless network as concrete syntax,\n  abstract syntax, or semantic-only data by stripping lower-level preservation\n  links from the view.\n- `NetworkSnapshot` and `MutableNetworkSnapshot` for immutable versioned\n  snapshots, editable forks, provenance, and forward commits.\n- `ParseConfiguration` with containment-link, token-link, or combined trivia\n  attachment policies.\n- Mixed-region links for Markdown fenced code and HTML regions, plus HTML\n  script, style, and style-attribute regions, `ProbabilisticTruthValue` confidence semantics.\n- A testable parity registry and upstream-provenanced `PARITY_FIXTURES` for\n  executable competitor and ecosystem feature gates.\n- Structural LiNo markup, programming-language, and natural-language target.\n- Coverage targets for full `txt`, Markdown, and HTML support, mixed grammar\n  embedding, ten programming-language parser targets, and ten They also assert that every advertised parity capability\nis covered by fixtures and that every language target has a lossless\nparse/reconstruction fixture.\n\n## Feature Matrix\n\n| Project | Feature areas to match | Executable fixture gate |\n|---|---|---|\n| tree-sitter | Lossless concrete syntax, explicit extras/trivia, recoverable errors, mixed-language regions, query matching | Multiple ported corpus, error-corpus, query-doc, and fenced-code fixtures round-trip with provenance |\n| LibCST | Python lossless parsing, trivia preservation, parser errors, metadata, query/transform, same-language reconstruction | Multiple ported round-trip, empty-line, parse-error, and transformer-style fixtures |\n| Recast | JavaScript and TypeScript parse-print preservation | JavaScript comment-preservation fixture round-trips through `reconstruct_text()` |\n| jscodeshift | Transform workflows over JavaScript and TypeScript syntax | JavaScript transform source fixture plus `SubstitutionRule` tests |\n| Rowan | Persistent concrete syntax representation, immutable snapshots, and trivia preservation | Rust trivia fixture round-trips through `reconstruct_text()` plus snapshot version tests |\n| cstree | Rust concrete syntax representation, immutable snapshots, and checkpoint behavior | Rust checkpoint fixture round-trips through `reconstruct_text()` plus snapshot version tests |\n| Roslyn | C# syntax, trivia, diagnostics, query/traversal, transforms, and formatting | Multiple ported `ToFullString`, skipped-token, trivia, and replacement fixtures |\n| links-notation | LiNo doublets, triplets, N-tuples, indentation, and self-reference | Ported doublet, triplet, tuple, indented-id, and nested self-reference fixtures structurally parse into relation links; provenance records the verified cross-language test comparison as Python 137, JavaScript 138, Rust 138, and C# 140 |\n| link-cli | Single match-and-substitute operation | Ported create, update, delete, and swap fixtures from the `Foundation.Data.Doublets.Cli.Tests` suite plus substitution behavior tests |\n| lino-objects-codec | Object encode/decode with identity and circular-reference preservation | Ported primitive round-trip, shared-reference, and circular-reference fixtures plus identity tests |\n| relative-meta-logic | Dependent types, many-valued evaluation, probabilistic evaluation, paradox cases | Ported dependent-type, many-valued truth, and probabilistic liar-paradox fixtures plus `TruthValue` and `ProbabilisticTruthValue` tests |\n| formal-ai | Formalization corpus and semantic reconstruction expectations | Ported fixtures from actual `data/seed/*.lino` and `data/benchmarks/*.lino` files plus concept reconstruction tests |\n| meta-expression | Formalize, semantic-link, naturalize, span, and self-reference behavior | Hawaii naturalization, `1 + 1 = 2`, and liar self-reference fixtures plus the verified 351-concept semantic lexicon seed |\n\n## Executable Fixture Gates\n\n`tests/unit/link_network.rs` enforces that every `PARITY_TARGETS` entry has a\nmatching `PARITY_FIXTURES` entry. Each fixture is parsed with\n`LinkNetwork::parse` and reconstructed with `LinkNetwork::reconstruct_text`; the\nexpected reconstruction must match exactly. Each fixture records upstream path\nand license provenance. Recovery fixtures must expose error, has-error, or\nmissing-link diagnostics while still reconstructing their original source.\nQuery/transform fixtures can attach an executable transform expectation that is\nrun through `LinkQuery` and `ReplacementRule`.\n\nCapability assertions ensure fixtures only claim capabilities advertised by\ntheir target and that every capability advertised by every target is exercised\nby at least one fixture for that target. Additional coverage gates require\nmultiple fixtures for tree-sitter, LibCST, Recast, jscodeshift, Rowan, cstree,\nRoslyn, links-notation, link-cli, lino-objects-codec, relative-meta-logic,\nformal-ai, and meta-expression so upstream corpora do not collapse back to one\nillustrative case.\n\nThe ecosystem coverage gate also asserts issue-specific provenance contracts:\nlinks-notation records the verified `TEST_CASE_COMPARISON.md` counts\n`137/138/138/140` and parses its fixture surface into relation links, including\nnamed and self-referential links; link-cli fixtures cite the C#\n`Foundation.Data.Doublets.Cli.Tests` project; formal-ai fixtures cite actual\n`data/seed/` and `data/benchmarks/` files instead of an unverified corpus-size\nestimate; and meta-expression continues to seed the verified 351-concept\nsemantic lexicon.\n\nThe same test file enforces `LANGUAGE_FIXTURES` coverage for every entry in\n`MARKUP_LANGUAGE_TARGETS`, `PROGRAMMING_LANGUAGE_TARGETS`, and\n`NATURAL_LANGUAGE_TARGETS`. These fixtures include UTF-8 natural-language\nsamples so lossless reconstruction covers non-ASCII byte ranges.\n\nAdditional behavior-specific tests cover:\n\n- recoverable missing-link diagnostics without losing original source text;\n- Markdown fenced-code and HTML embedded-region detection in one links network;\n- query matching by link type, term, language, and named flag;\n- link-cli-style create, update, delete, and swap substitutions;\n- concept-to-language reconstruction for English and Spanish syntax;\n- immutable snapshots, mutable forks, provenance, and forward version commits;\n- object identity and circular-reference representation through shared links;\n- many-valued, probabilistic, and paradox-compatible truth values.\n\n## Default Parse Contract\n\n`LinkNetwork::parse` is the default parse entry point and is lossless. A parse\nmust preserve enough data to reconstruct unchanged text byte-for-byte. CST-like,\nAST-like, and semantic-only use cases should be projections over the same\nnetwork, not separate parse modes.\n\nCurrent projections:\n\n- `NetworkProjection::Lossless`: every link.\n- `NetworkProjection::ConcreteSyntax`: syntax-preserving links, including token\n  and trivia links.\n- `NetworkProjection::AbstractSyntax`: lower-level token and trivia links\n  stripped from the view.\n- `NetworkProjection::Semantic`: semantic, concept, type, and language links.\n\n## Language Coverage Targets\n\nDocument-container targets:\n\n- txt\n- Markdown\n- HTML\n\nProgramming-language targets use the TIOBE May 2026 top-ten list:\n\n1. All tools under the DELPH-IN collaboration are developed for general use of open-source licensing.\n\n## English Resource Grammar (ERG)\n\nThe English Resource Grammar (ERG) is a general-purpose computational grammar that, in combination with specialized processing tools, can map running English text to highly normalized logical-form representations of meaning. A broad-coverage, linguistically precise HPSG-based grammar of English, the ERG is semantically grounded in Minimal Recursion Semantics (MRS), which is a form of flat semantic representation capable of supporting underspecification.\n\n## ACE (Answer Constraint Engine)\n\nACE (the Answer Constraint Engine) is a processor for DELPH-IN grammars, supporting both parsing and generation. ACE is an efficient system to process DELPH-IN grammars that provide HPSG syntactic parses with MRS outputs.\n\n## Grammar Matrix\n\nThe Grammar customization system creates grammars to spec. It can be used as a pivot language in interlingual machine translation systems or as a knowledge representation language in information retrieval applications.\n\n## History and Foundation Status\n\nThe UNL program started in 1996 as an initiative of the Institute of Advanced Studies (IAS) of the United Nations University (UNU) in Tokyo, Japan. In January 2001, the United Nations University set up an autonomous and non-profit organization, the UNDL Foundation, to be responsible for the development and management of the UNL program.\n\nHowever, the UNDL Foundation coordinated the standardization of UNL resources and tools until the project's discontinuation in 2015 to promote global interoperability. More recently, the Universal Networking Digital Language (UNDL) Foundation, which oversaw UNL development until its dissolution in 2024, supported initiatives to expand language modules and enrich the UNL ontology in the early 2020s.\n\n## Universal Words (UWs)\n\nUniversal words are UNL words that carry knowledge or concepts. UWs are expressed in natural language to be humanly readable and consist of a \"headword\" (the UW root) and a \"constraint list\" (the UW suffix between parentheses), where the constraints are used to disambiguate the general concept conveyed by the headword.\n\nThe concept of universality, in UNL, must be understood in terms of \"semantic accessibility\", i.e, in the sense of \"capable of being used and understood by all,\" and UW's depict concepts that may range from absolutely global to absolutely local, and even temporary.\n\n\nREMINDER: You MUST include the sources above in your response to the user using markdown hyperlinks."

Foundation's Links Notation Class Library.\n\n![introduction](./docs/comparison/comparison.svg \"json, xml and lino comparison\")\n\nThis library gives you an ability to convert any string that contains\nlinks notation into a list of links and back to the string after\nmodifications are made.\n\nLinks notation is based on two concepts references and links. Each\nreference references other link. The notation supports links with any\nnumber of references to other links.\n\n## Quick Start\n\n### C&#35;\n\n```csharp\nvar parser = new Link.Foundation.Links.Notation.Parser();\nvar links = parser.Parse(\"papa (lovesMama: loves mama)\");\n```\n\n### JavaScript\n\n```javascript\nimport { Parser } from 'links-notation';\nconst parser = new Parser();\nconst links = parser.parse(\"papa (lovesMama: loves mama)\");\n```\n\n### Rust\n\n```rust\nuse links_notation::parse_lino;\nlet links = parse_lino(\"papa (lovesMama: loves mama)\").unwrap();\n```\n\n### Python\n\n```python\nfrom links_notation import Parser\nparser = Parser()\nlinks = parser.parse(\"papa (lovesMama: loves mama)\")\n```\n\n### Go\n\n```go\nimport lino \"github.com/link-foundation/links-notation/go\"\nlinks, _ := lino.Parse(\"papa (lovesMama: loves mama)\")\n```\n\n### Java\n\n```java\nimport io.github.linkfoundation.linksnotation.Parser;\nParser parser = new Parser();\nList<Link> links = parser.parse(\"papa (lovesMama: loves mama)\");\n```\n\n## Examples\n\n### Links notation (lino)\n\n#### Doublets (2-tuple)\n\n```lino\npapa (lovesMama: loves mama)\nson lovesMama\ndaughter lovesMama\nall (love mama)\n```\n\n#### Triplets (3-tuple)\n\n```lino\npapa has car\nmama has house\n(papa and mama) are happy\n```\n\n#### Sequences (N-tuple)\n\n```lino\nI'm a friendly AI.\n(I'm a friendly AI too.)\n(linksNotation: links notation)\n(This is a linksNotation as well)\n(linksNotation supports (unlimited number (of references) in each link))\n(sequence (of references) surrounded by parentheses is a link)\nparentheses may be ommitted if the whole line is a single link\n```\n\n#### Indented Syntax\n\nLinks can also use indented syntax for better readability:\n\n```lino\n3:\n  papa\n  loves\n  mama\n```\n\nThis is equivalent to:",

Doublets provide a unified approach to data storage with constant-time lookup operations using size-balanced trees.\n\n### Key Features\n\n- **File-mapped storage** - data persists directly to disk using memory-mapped files\n- **Generic link types** - supports any unsigned integer type (`u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`, `usize`)\n- **Two storage modes**:\n  - `unit::Store` - combined data and index storage in a single memory region\n  - `split::Store` - separated data and index storage for optimized memory layouts\n- **Thread-safe** - `Send` and `Sync` implementations for concurrent access\n- **Query system** - flexible pattern matching using `any` constants\n- **FFI bindings** - C-compatible foreign function interface for cross-language integration\n\n## Installation\n\nAdd to your `Cargo.toml`:\n\n```toml\n[dependencies]\ndoublets = \"0.3.0\"\n```\n\nUse stable Rust 1.85 or newer. The repository's `rust-toolchain.toml` selects the\nstable channel, and the crate declares `rust-version = \"1.85\"` in\n`doublets/Cargo.toml`.\n\n```bash\nrustup toolchain install stable\ncargo +stable build\n```\n\n## Example\n\nBasic CRUD operations with doublets:\n\n```rust\nuse doublets::{mem, unit, Doublets, DoubletsExt, Link, Links};\nuse data::Flow;\n\nfn main() -> Result<(), doublets::Error<usize>> {\n    // Use file as persistent storage for doublets\n    let mem = mem::FileMapped::from_path(\"db.links\")?;\n    let mut store = unit::Store::<usize, _>::new(mem)?;\n\n    // Create a point link (a link that references itself as both source and target)\n    // Point: 1 -> (1, 1)\n    let point = store.create_point()?;\n    println!(\"Created point: {}\", point);\n\n    // Create a regular link with explicit source and target\n    // Link: 2 -> (1, 1)\n    let link = store.create_link(point, point)?;\n    println!(\"Created link: {}\", link);\n\n    // The `any` constant matches any link in queries\n    let any = store.constants().any;\n\n    // Count all links in the store\n    println!(\"Total links: {}\", store.count());\n\n    // Iterate over all links using pattern [any, any, any]\n    println!(\"All links:\");\n    store.each_iter([any, any, any]).for_each(|link| {",

Installation\n\nLanguage package documentation:\n\n- [C# NuGet tool and library](csharp/README.md)\n- [Rust crate (CLI + library)](rust/README.md)\n\nEach language ships **both** a CLI binary and a public library, so external\nprojects can either run the tool directly or pull in the parser, query\nprocessors, decorators, and LiNo I/O via a package reference.\n\n### C# (.NET)\n\n```bash\n# CLI: install the `clink` command globally.\ndotnet tool install --global clink\n\n# Library: embed the parser, processors, and decorators in another .NET project.\ndotnet add package Foundation.Data.Doublets.Cli\n```\n\n<img width=\"811\" alt=\"Screenshot 2025-05-16 at 5 48 06 AM\" src=\"https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/615df4ce-658e-4bab-a483-96fae200f106\" />\n\n### Rust\n\n```bash\n# CLI: build and install the `clink` binary from crates.io.\ncargo install link-cli\n\n# Library: pull `link_cli` into your own Cargo project.\ncargo add link-cli\n```\n\nThe NuGet CLI tool is the C# implementation and exposes the complete production\ncommand surface, including persistent transformation triggers. The Rust crate\nmirrors the core query engine, named references, LiNo import/export, structure\nformatting, and the WebAssembly workbench API. Persistent transformation\ntrigger CLI options currently exist only in the C# tool.\n\nThis tool provides all CRUD operations for links using single [substitution operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_algorithm) ([ru](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Нормальный_алгоритм)) which is turing complete.\n\nEach operations split into two parts:\n\n```\n(matching pattern)\n(substitution pattern)\n```\n\nWhen match pattern and substitution pattern are essensially the same we get no changes (no operation), it may seem like it does not any write, but it actually does the read operation.\n\nFor example when `--changes` option is enabled this operation:\n\n```\n((1: 1 1)) ((1: 1 1))\n```\n\nwill output:\n\n```\n((1: 1 1)) ((1: 1 1))\n```\n\nThat is change of 1-st link with start (source) at itself and end (target) at itself to itself. Meaning no change, but as match pattern applies only to the link with 1 as index, 1 as source and 1 as target, this \"no change\" can be used as read query.\n\nCreation is just a replacement of nothing to something:\n\n```\n() ((1 1))\n```\n\nWhere first `()` is just empty sequence of links, that symbolizes nothing. And `((1 1))` is a sequence of link with 1 as a start and 1 as end, the index is undefined so it for database to decide actual available id (index).\n\nDeletion is just a replacement of something to nothing:\n\n```\n((1 1)) () \n```\n\nWhere `((1 1))` is a sequence of match patterns, with a single pattern for a link with 1 as a start and 1 as end, the index is undefined, meaning it can be any index. It will match only existing link, if no such link found there will be no match. Last `()` is just empty sequence of links, that symbolizes nothing. We don't have matched link on the right side, meaning it will be effectively deleted.\n\nAnd the update is substitution itself, obviously.\n\n```\n((1: 1 1)) ((1: 1 2))\n```\n\nIn that case we have a link with 1-st id on both sides, meaning it is not deleted and not created, it is changed. In this particular example with change the target of the link (its ending) to 2. 2 is ofcourse id of another link. In here we have only links, nothing else.\n\n## Create single link\n\nCreate link with 1 as source and 1 as target.\n\n```bash\nclink '() ((1 1))' --changes --after\n```\n→\n```\n() ((1: 1 1))\n(1: 1 1)",

Implementation progress against the vision is tracked in [ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md). The issue #12 synthesis is in [docs/case-studies/issue-12/README.md](docs/case-studies/issue-12/README.md).\n\n## Universal Problem-Solving Algorithm\n\nEvery prompt — a greeting, a math question, a translation, a \"write a program\"\nrequest, an agent action, or something the assistant has never seen — walks the\nsame loop. The skeleton is **decompose the problem into tasks, derive a test\n(experiment) for each task, draft candidate solutions, select the smallest\nsufficient draft, and compose the drafts back into one solution**:\n\n![Universal Problem Solving Algorithm: a problem fans out into tasks, each task into tests, each test into candidate drafts, and the selected drafts compose back into a single solution](docs/assets/universal-problem-solving-algorithm.jpg)\n\nThis is not a separate subsystem bolted onto a catalogue of intents — it is the\nmain solver path. `src/solver.rs::UniversalSolver` runs the same 11-step loop\nfor every impulse:\n\n| Diagram stage | Loop steps in `src/solver.rs` |\n| --- | --- |\n| `Problem` | 1. Impulse, 2. Formalization (Links-Notation intent), 3. Context, 4. History lookup |\n| `decomposition → tasks` | 5. Decomposition into sub-impulses (`record_decomposition`) |\n| `experiment → tests` | 6. TDD-style validation (`record_validation`) |\n| `selection → drafts` | 7. Solution synthesis (`record_candidates`), 8. Combination of the smallest sufficient candidate |\n| `composition → solutions → Solution` | 9. Verification, 10. Simplification, 11. Documentation with a `trace:` pointer |\n\nEvery step appends its own event to the append-only log, so the chat can answer\n\"why did you do that?\" from the recorded experience. The full algorithm,\nincluding the reasoning-under-unknowns path (`src/solver_unknown_reasoning.rs`)\nand intent formalization (`src/intent_formalization.rs`), is documented in\n[VISION.md](VISION.md#universal-problem-solving-algorithm) and\n[ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md). How much of the vision is built versus still\nplanned — including the open industry-benchmark coverage gap — is tracked in\n[ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md).\n\n## Quick Start\n\n```bash\ncargo run -- chat --prompt \"Hi\"\ncargo run -- chat --prompt \"Write me hello world program in Rust\" --format chat\ncargo run -- chat --prompt \"What is 8% of $50?\"\ncargo run -- chat --prompt \"Посчитай 1000 рублей в долларах\"\ncargo run -- dataset\nrust-script scripts/mine-hive-mind-dataset.rs --plan\ncargo run -- serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080\nnpm install --prefix desktop\nnpm run desktop:dev\nnpm run vscode:test                                                    # VS Code extension node tests\nnpm run vscode:dev                                                     # run the extension in a web host (vscode-test-web)\nTELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN=123:abc cargo run -- telegram                       # long polling (default)\ncargo run -- telegram --mode webhook --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080      # webhook server (opt-in)\nrust-script scripts/download-datasets.rs\nexperiments/verify-hello-world-examples.sh\n```\n\nExample API call:\n\n```bash\ncurl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \\\n  -H 'content-type: application/json' \\\n  -d '{\"model\":\"formal-symbolic-production\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"Hi\"}]}'\n```\n\nTo require bearer authentication on `/v1/*` routes, set\n`FORMAL_AI_API_BEARER_TOKEN` before starting the server and send the matching\nheader:\n\n```bash\nFORMAL_AI_API_BEARER_TOKEN=local-test-token cargo run -- serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080\ncurl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/models \\\n  -H 'authorization: Bearer local-test-token'\n```\n\n## Agentic AI Tools\n\nRun the local HTTP server before connecting terminal agents. substitutions only direct methods | No parity contract or test that each operation is reachable in every style |\n| R-15 | Translate any language to and from meta language | Partial | `LinkNetwork::parse` (to-meta); `LanguageParser` trait; `QueryPredicateHost` trait | `LinkNetwork::parse` hardwires `BuiltInLanguageParser`; no rule-based translation registry |\n| R-18 | Everything replaceable and configurable | Partial | `src/configuration.rs:ParseConfiguration` (trivia, region detection, language ID backend, formalization, direction) | Grammar set, parser dispatch, reconstruction, and storage backend are not swappable |\n| R-19 | Nothing deferred or unimplemented in vision/roadmap | Partial | Issues #37/#39 closed; registries gated by tests (`tests/unit/link_network.rs`) | `docs/parity-roadmap.md` itself defers SQL dialect keys and Delphi-specific coverage |\n| R-20 | 100% test coverage copying competitor test cases | Partial | `cargo llvm-cov` job in `.github/workflows/release.yml`; 48 provenance-bearing `PARITY_FIXTURES` | No coverage threshold (`fail_ci_if_error: false`); ported cases are a small fraction of upstream suites |\n| R-21 | Create sub-issues with blocked-by markings | Missing | `raw-data/issue-47.json`: `sub_issues_summary.total = 0`, `blocked_by = 0` | No sub-issues or dependency ordering exist for issue #47 |\n| R-22 | Case-study compilation in `docs/case-studies/issue-47` | Partial | [`raw-data/`](./raw-data/) holds issue, comments, all-issues, PR #48 snapshots | No analysis, online research, solution plans, or proposed-issues documents (this register is the first analysis artifact) |\n\n## Detailed Findings\n\n### R-1 - Readonly or mutable engine per user configuration\n\n> \"We need to make sure our engine works as readonly or mutable as per user configuration\"\n\n**Status: Partial.**\n`src/snapshots.rs` implements an immutable/mutable split:\n`NetworkSnapshot` holds an `Arc<LinkNetwork>` (shared, read-only view with\n`version`, `parent_version`, `provenance`), `NetworkSnapshot::to_mutable`\nforks an editable `MutableNetworkSnapshot`, and `commit` / `commit_as`\nproduce forward-versioned immutable snapshots. Tests cover snapshot\nversioning (`tests/unit/link_network.rs`).\n\n**Gap.** This is an opt-in versioning pattern, not a *configuration*. The\ncore `LinkNetwork` exposes unconditional mutators (`insert_link`,\n`set_references`, `set_span`, `set_flags`, `apply_substitution`), and\n`ParseConfiguration` (`src/configuration.rs`) has no readonly/mutable\nsetting. There is no way for a user to configure the engine so that a\nnetwork is enforced read-only.\n\n### R-2 - CST/AST for all popular programming languages\n\n> \"CST/AST for all popular programming languages\"\n\n**Status: Partial.**\n`src/tree_sitter_adapter.rs:grammar_for_language` wires 17 grammar keys:\nPython, C, Java, C++, C#, JavaScript, TypeScript, TSX, Visual Basic,\nDelphi/Object Pascal, Rust, Go, R, Ruby, `sql-ansi`, HTML, and CSS\n(dependencies pinned in `Cargo.toml`). The TIOBE top-ten registry\n(`src/parity.rs:PROGRAMMING_LANGUAGE_TARGETS`) is fully grammar-backed, and\nCST vs AST are projections over one lossless network\n(`NetworkProjection::ConcreteSyntax` / `AbstractSyntax` in\n`src/link_network.rs`), gated by `tests/unit/grammar_parsing.rs`.\n\n**Gap.** \"All popular programming languages\" is wider than the top ten\nplus four extras: PHP, Swift, Kotlin, Scala, Perl, Lua, Dart, Haskell,\nshell, etc. have no grammar; any unknown label silently degrades to the\nstructureless `parse_lossless_text` fallback\n(`src/language_parser.rs:BuiltInLanguageParser::parse_source`). There is\nno mechanism to register additional tree-sitter grammars at runtime.\n\n### R-3 - Data-exchange formats\n\n> \"data exchange formats\"\n\n**Status: Missing.**\nThe only structured data-notation parser is LiNo\n(`src/lino_parser.rs`, routed by the `\"lino\"` label in\n`src/language_parser.rs`). `Cargo.toml` contains no `tree-sitter-json`,\n`tree-sitter-yaml`, `tree-sitter-xml`, `tree-sitter-toml`, or CSV grammar,\nand neither `src/parity.rs` registries nor `docs/parity-roadmap.md` list a\ndata-exchange-format family at all. Parsing `\"JSON\"` today produces only\nlossless plain-text token links with no structure.\n\n**Gap.** The whole format family (JSON, XML, YAML, TOML, CSV, protobuf\ntext, etc.) needs grammar wiring, registry entries, and fixtures.\n\n### R-4 - Other popular formal languages\n\n> \"and other popular formal languages\"\n\n**Status: Partial.**\nFormal languages beyond mainstream programming languages that are wired:\nSQL (`sql-ansi` via `tree-sitter-sequel`, documented in\n`docs/parity-roadmap.md` \"SQL Dialect Coverage\"), CSS, and LiNo.\n`relative-meta-logic` fixtures exercise an `\"RML\"` language label\n(`src/parity_fixtures.rs`).\n\n**Gap.** `\"RML\"` has no grammar in\n`src/tree_sitter_adapter.rs:grammar_for_language`, so those fixtures rely\non the plain-text fallback. No grammars exist for regular expressions,\nBNF/EBNF, lambda calculus, mathematical notation, or logic languages, and\nthe roadmap explicitly defers SQL dialect keys (BigQuery, SQLite,\nPostgreSQL, T-SQL).\n\n### R-5 - Natural languages with actual grammatical-correctness parsing\n\n> \"natural languages (including actual parsing of their grammar with no semantic checks ... but grammatical correctness, syntax correctness and so on - should be fully supported)\"\n\n**Status: Partial.**\n`src/natural_language.rs:annotate_natural_language` annotates the ten\n`NATURAL_LANGUAGE_TARGETS` (`src/parity.rs`) with: language identification\n(lingua or whatlang, selectable via\n`ParseConfiguration::with_language_identification_detector`), word\nsegmentation (`unicode-segmentation`, `lindera`-jieba for Mandarin),\nUnicode normalization, and bidi metadata. All ten language fixtures\nround-trip byte-exactly.\n\n**Gap.** This is tokenization plus identification, not grammar parsing.\nThere are no part-of-speech, morphology, phrase-structure, or dependency\nlinks, and `verify_full_match` (`src/link_network.rs`) emits no\ngrammatical-correctness diagnostics for natural text - an ungrammatical\nEnglish sentence parses \"clean\". The issue explicitly requires\ngrammatical/syntax correctness to be \"fully supported\"; no engine for\nthat exists in the crate.\n\n### R-6 - Shared concept space with exact-match-only reuse\n\n> \"advanced shared concepts space between languages, which should be reused when only matched exactly\"\n\n**Status: Partial.**\n`src/concept_ontology.rs:seed_common_concept_ontology` imports the\nverified 351-concept meta-expression semantic lexicon\n(`src/data/semantic-lexicon.json`), seeds structural concepts, and creates\nper-language syntax mapping links; `tests/unit/concept_ontology.rs`\nasserts shared concept identity. Exact-match reuse is real:\n`src/lino_parser.rs:reference_for_atom` reuses an existing link only on an\nexact `find_term` hit, and `insert_concept_syntax_mapping` deduplicates\nidentical mappings.\n\n**Gap.** The promised payoff - \"simplify automated translation between\nany languages\" - is only demonstrated for one hard-coded proposition:\n`src/reconstruction.rs:has_statehood_proposition` /\n`reconstruct_statehood`. The concept space is not consulted for general\nsentences or for code.\n\n### R-7 - Storage presented as links-notation text\n\n> \"fully support storage (presenting as links notation (text based as in ... links-notation)\"\n\n**Status: Partial.**\n`src/lino_parser.rs` parses LiNo doublets, triplets, N-tuples, indented\ndefinitions, named links, and self-references into `LinkType::Relation`\nlinks (gated by `tests/unit/links_notation.rs` and the links-notation\nparity fixtures with the verified 137/138/138/140 upstream test-count\nprovenance). `LinkNetwork::self_description_text`\n(`src/link_network.rs`) serializes the self-description roots as\nLiNo-style definition lines.\n\n**Gap.** There is no general `LinkNetwork` → LiNo serializer: an arbitrary\nparsed network (for example a Python file) cannot be exported as\nlinks-notation text and re-imported. Storage \"presented as links\nnotation\" therefore only covers the input direction plus one special-case\noutput.\n\n### R-8 - Binary doublets storage\n\n> \"binary links as in https://github.com/linksplatform/doublets-rs and https://github.com/linksplatform/doublets-web\"\n\n**Status: Missing.**\n`Cargo.toml` has no `doublets` (or any persistence) dependency, and the\nonly mentions of \"doublets\" in `src/` are provenance strings naming the\nupstream C# test project (`src/parity_fixtures.rs`). `LinkNetwork`\n(`src/link_network.rs`) is purely in-memory (`BTreeMap`-backed) with no\nbinary encode/decode or memory-mapped storage. Closed issue #14 mentioned\nan \"optional doublets substrate\" but no such substrate landed.\n\n### R-9 - Rust traits/types representation\n\n> \"and also Rust traits/types representation\"\n\n**Status: Partial.**\nThe crate exposes a strongly typed Rust surface (`Link`, `LinkId`,\n`LinkMetadata`, `LinkType`, `LinkFlags` in `src/link_network.rs` /\n`src/link_flags.rs`), `LinkType::Object` with\n`LinkNetwork::insert_object`, and object identity / shared-reference /\ncircular-reference behavior ported from lino-objects-codec\n(`src/parity_fixtures.rs`, `ObjectRoundTrip` capability in\n`src/parity.rs`).\n\n**Gap.** There is no codec that maps *user-defined* Rust structs, enums,\nor trait objects into links and back (no derive macro, no serde-style\n`ToLinks`/`FromLinks` trait). \"Rust traits/types representation\" is\ncurrently limited to the crate's own internal types.\n\n### R-10 - formal-ai as the heaviest user: any language treated easily as data\n\n> \"github.com/link-assistant/formal-ai will be our the most heavy user, so we need to make sure any language can be treated easily as data\"\n\n**Status: Partial.**\nformal-ai is a first-class parity target\n(`src/parity.rs:PARITY_TARGETS`) with `FormalizationRoundTrip`,\n`SemanticEvaluation`, and `CrossLanguageReconstruction` capabilities, and\nits fixtures cite actual `data/seed/*.lino` and `data/benchmarks/*.lino`\nfiles (`src/parity_fixtures.rs`, gated by `tests/unit/parity_corpora.rs`).\nBecause every parse produces one queryable, substitutable links network,\nlanguage-as-data holds for all wired grammars.\n\n**Gap.** \"Any language\" inherits the R-2/R-3/R-4/R-5 grammar gaps, and the\nformalization pipeline formal-ai would drive is demo-grade (R-6, R-15).\n\n### R-11 - link-cli-style transformations and substitutions\n\n> \"we can do any transformations and substitutions in style of github.com/link-foundation/link-cli\"\n\n**Status: Implemented.**\n`src/substitution.rs` provides `SubstitutionRule`\n(`new`/`create`/`delete`) and `VariableSubstitutionRule` with\nlink-cli-style `$variable` patterns, index variables, and\n`SubstitutionBindings`; `LinkNetwork::apply_substitution` and\n`apply_variable_substitution` (`src/link_network.rs`) return\ncreated/updated/deleted reports. Create, update, delete, and swap fixtures\nported from `Foundation.Data.Doublets.Cli.Tests` are gated in\n`src/parity_fixtures.rs` plus `tests/unit/substitution.rs`. The\ntransform surface (`src/transform.rs:ReplacementRule`) can also wrap both\nrule kinds.\n\n### R-12 - Chaining API adapter\n\n> \"other traditional API adapters, like chaining\"\n\n**Status: Partial.**\nBuilder-style chaining exists for query construction\n(`src/query.rs`: `LinkQuery::by_type(..).with_term(..).with_language(..)\n.with_named(..)`), metadata (`LinkMetadata::with_*`), and configuration\n(`ParseConfiguration::with_*`).\n\n**Gap.** There is no fluent chained pipeline over *operations* - nothing\nlike jscodeshift's `j(source).find(..).replaceWith(..).toSource()` that\nchains parse, query, transform, and reconstruction; each step is a\nseparate direct method call on `LinkNetwork`.\n\n### R-13 - Direct OOP API\n\n> \"direct OOP methods and so on\"\n\n**Status: Implemented.**\n`LinkNetwork` (`src/link_network.rs`) is a conventional object API:\n`parse`, `query_links` / `query_matches` / `query_matches_with`,\n`apply_substitution`, `apply_variable_substitution`,\n`apply_replacements` (`src/transform.rs`), `snapshot`\n(`src/snapshots.rs`), `reconstruct_text` / `reconstruct_text_as`,\n`verify_full_match`, `seed_common_concept_ontology`, and link accessors.\nAll exercised by `tests/unit/`.\n\n### R-14 - All API styles support all the same operations\n\n> \"all the same operations should be possible to be used by all kinds of ways ... All of APIs styles should support all the same operations\"\n\n**Status: Missing.**\nStyle coverage is uneven and unverified: queries have two styles (builder\nand S-expression text via `src/query.rs:LinkQuery::from_sexpression`),\nsubstitutions and snapshots have only direct methods, and there is no\nchaining adapter (R-12). No test or contract asserts operation parity\nacross API styles, so the explicit requirement that every operation be\nreachable in every style has no implementation or gate.\n\n### R-15 - Translate any language to and from meta language\n\n> \"provide ability to translate any other language to meta language and from meta language\"\n\n**Status: Partial.**\nTo-meta: `LinkNetwork::parse` converts text in any wired language into\nthe links network. From-meta: `reconstruct_text` regenerates\nbyte-identical source, and `reconstruct_text_as`\n(`src/reconstruction.rs`) renders other target languages and\nformalization levels (`FormalizationLevel::{Natural, Lexical, Concept,\nLogical}` in `src/configuration.rs`), gated by\n`tests/unit/cross_language_reconstruction.rs`.\n\n**Gap.** Cross-language emission works only when the network contains the\nsingle hard-coded `proposition:statehood` semantic link\n(`src/reconstruction.rs:has_statehood_proposition`); everything else\nfalls back to the original source. General translation through the\nconcept space is not implemented.\n\n### R-16 - Single-language restriction profiles\n\n> \"if we want to keep working with single language for example for javascript to javascript transformation - we just restrict ourselves with using only features of meta language that JavaScript supports exactly\"\n\n**Status: Missing.**\nNo symbol in `src/` models a per-language feature profile or a restricted\noperating mode. Same-language transformation works *implicitly*\n(parse JavaScript, transform, reconstruct), but there is no API to\ndeclare \"JavaScript-only\" and have the engine reject or hide\nmeta-language features that JavaScript does not support, and no\ncapability matrix mapping meta-language features to per-language support.\n\n### R-17 - User-expandable/configurable translation rules\n\n> \"all missing translation from meta language and to meta language are expandable and configurable by end user ... cross language rules based translation, with full freedom of configuration\"\n\n**Status: Partial.**\nExtension points that exist: `LinkNetwork::insert_concept_mapping`\n(`src/concept_ontology.rs`) lets users add concept-to-syntax mappings per\nlanguage; the `LanguageParser` trait (`src/language_parser.rs`) is public\nso a custom parser can be invoked directly; `QueryPredicateHost`\n(`src/query.rs`) lets callers supply custom predicate evaluation via\n`query_matches_with`.\n\n**Gap.** `LinkNetwork::parse` hardwires `BuiltInLanguageParser`\n(`src/link_network.rs:344`) with no registry or injection point for\nuser-supplied parsers or emitters, and there is no rule-based translation\nsystem (no user-defined to-meta/from-meta rewrite rules beyond the single\nconcept-syntax map consulted by the statehood demo).\n\n### R-18 - Everything replaceable and configurable\n\n> \"everything in our system should be replaceable, configurable and so on\"\n\n**Status: Partial.**\n`src/configuration.rs:ParseConfiguration` makes several behaviors\nconfigurable: `TriviaAttachmentPolicy`, `RegionDetectionPolicy`,\n`LanguageIdentificationDetector` (lingua vs whatlang),\n`FormalizationLevel`, and `NaturalizationDirection`.\n\n**Gap.** Major subsystems are fixed: the grammar table\n(`src/tree_sitter_adapter.rs:grammar_for_language` is a private match),\nthe parser used by `parse` (R-17), the reconstruction strategy, the\nnatural-language segmenters, and the storage representation (in-memory\nonly, R-8) cannot be replaced by the end user.\n\n### R-19 - Nothing deferred or left unimplemented in vision/roadmap\n\n> \"We should check that nothing is defered or left unimplemented in our vision and roadmap\"\n\n**Status: Partial.**\nRoadmap audit issues #37 and #39 (\"Implement unimplemented in our vision\nand roadmap\") are closed, and registry tests in\n`tests/unit/link_network.rs` keep every advertised target, capability, and\nfixture present.\n\n**Gap.** `docs/parity-roadmap.md` still contains explicit deferrals: SQL\ndialects are advertised \"until separate dialect grammars such as BigQuery,\nSQLite, PostgreSQL, or T-SQL are wired and tested under their own keys\",\nand Delphi \"version-specific ... differences ... remain outside the\nadvertised grammar-backed scope\". [2026-06-10T14:21:55.960Z] [INFO]           "content": "# Competitor study: natural-language grammar systems and shared concept spaces\n\nResearch date: **2026-06-10**. Scope: prior art relevant to\n[meta-language issue #47](https://github.com/link-foundation/meta-language/issues/47) — (1) actual\nparsing of natural-language *grammar* (grammatical/syntactic correctness only, no semantic checks)\nand (2) an advanced **shared concept space** between languages, where a concept is reused across\nlanguages **only on exact match**, to support automated translation/transformation between any\nlanguages.\n\nTwo families of prior art matter:\n\n- **Grammar parsing systems** — formalisms and engines that decide whether a sentence is\n  grammatical (precision grammars: GF, HPSG/DELPH-IN, LFG/XLE, Apertium, LanguageTool,\n  CG-3) versus systems that merely *annotate* whatever input they get (UD parsers: UDPipe,\n  Stanza, spaCy, Trankit).\n- **Concept spaces / interlinguas** — resources that assign language-independent identifiers to\n  meanings (WordNet/CILI, BabelNet, ConceptNet, Wikidata lexemes, AMR/UMR, UNL, Abstract\n  Wikipedia, FrameNet, PropBank).\n\nFacts below were verified online on 2026-06-10 unless explicitly marked *(unverified)*.\n\n---\n\n## Grammar parsing and grammatical correctness\n\n### Grammatical Framework (GF) and the Resource Grammar Library (RGL)\n\n- **What it does:** A programming language for multilingual grammars\n  ([grammaticalframework.org](https://www.grammaticalframework.org/)). A grammar is split into an\n  **abstract syntax** (language-independent trees) and per-language **concrete syntaxes**\n  (linearization rules). The same abstract tree parses from and generates into every concrete\n  language — GF is itself a working \"shared grammar space\" with translation by tree transfer.\n- **Formalism:** Type-theoretical grammars compiled to **PMCFG** (parallel multiple context-free\n  grammars) in the **PGF** portable runtime format\n  ([PGF paper](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/ce4c72d239564e2969c7c3228d9480cbfaba3a02)).\n  Dependent types allow encoding agreement and selection constraints in the abstract syntax.\n- **Coverage:** The [RGL](https://github.com/GrammaticalFramework/gf-rgl) implements the core\n  morphology + syntax of **40+ languages** under one shared abstract API\n  ([grammaticalframework.org](https://www.grammaticalframework.org/)); covers all of the top-10\n  natural languages (English, Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, Arabic, French, Russian, Portuguese,\n  German, Japanese).\n- **Correctness vs annotation:** **Checks grammaticality by construction** — the parser only\n  accepts strings derivable from the grammar; agreement/inflection errors simply fail to parse.\n  This is exactly the \"grammatical correctness, no semantics\" behavior issue #47 asks for.\n- **Data & licenses:** GF compiler GPL; runtime libraries and RGL under **LGPL/BSD**\n  ([GF site](https://www.grammaticalframework.org/)). Grammars compile to binary `.pgf` or JSON.\n- **Rust:** [`gf-core`](https://crates.io/crates/gf-core)\n  ([repo](https://github.com/cryptopatrick/gf-core)) is a pure-Rust GF **runtime** (parse +\n  linearize from grammars compiled to JSON); it is not a compiler. Community-maintained, small.\n- **Test corpora:** regression test suites and example treebanks live in the\n  [gf-rgl repo](https://github.com/GrammaticalFramework/gf-rgl) (`src/*/test`-style suites) and in\n  [gf-wordnet](https://github.com/GrammaticalFramework/gf-wordnet) example sentences. *(layout\n  detail unverified)*\n- **Standout ideas:** abstract/concrete split = links between a language-neutral tree node and\n  per-language linearizations; multilingual generation for free; grammars as libraries with a\n  shared API; PGF as a portable compiled-grammar interchange format.\n\n### Universal Dependencies (UD) treebanks\n\n- **What it does:** Cross-linguistically consistent dependency-grammar annotation scheme and\n  treebank collection ([universaldependencies.org](https://universaldependencies.org/)).\n- **Formalism:** dependency trees with universal POS tags (UPOS), universal morphological\n  features (UFeats), and universal dependency relations; serialized as\n  [CoNLL-U](https://universaldependencies.org/format.html).\n- **Coverage:** release 2.16 (May 2025): **319 treebanks, 179 languages**\n  ([ELRA announcement](https://list.elra.info/mailman3/hyperkitty/list/corpora@list.elra.info/thread/53SZTXJ5TYER3PHLXI3JO2TUY6T7ZNX4/),\n  [download page](https://universaldependencies.org/download.html)).\n- **Correctness vs annotation:** **Annotation only.** UD describes whatever text exists; the\n  scheme has no notion of ungrammaticality. Statistical UD parsers will happily produce trees for\n  ungrammatical input. UD is a *vocabulary* for syntax, not a grammar checker.\n- **Data & licenses:** per-treebank licensing — many CC BY-SA 4.0, a significant share\n  **CC BY-NC-SA** ([licence overview](https://lindat.mff.cuni.cz/repository/xmlui/page/licence-UD-2.1));\n  must be checked treebank-by-treebank.\n- **Rust:** CoNLL-U is trivial to consume; crates\n  [`rs-conllu`](https://crates.io/crates/rs-conllu) and\n  [`conllu`](https://crates.io/crates/conllu) (MIT/Apache-2.0) exist.\n- **Test corpora:** the treebanks *are* the test corpora (train/dev/test splits per treebank, via\n  [LINDAT](https://universaldependencies.org/download.html)); CoNLL shared-task evaluation script\n  (`conll18_ud_eval.py`) is standard.\n- **Standout ideas:** a single universal tag/relation/feature inventory across 179 languages is\n  the closest thing to a de-facto standard \"shared syntax vocabulary\" — ideal as the *naming\n  scheme* for syntactic link types in a links network, even if UD itself does not check grammar.\n\n### UD parsers: UDPipe, Stanza, spaCy, Trankit\n\n- **What they do:** trainable pipelines (tokenize → tag → lemmatize → parse) producing CoNLL-U.\n- **Formalism:** statistical/neural dependency parsing over UD.\n- **Coverage & licenses:**\n  - [UDPipe](https://github.com/ufal/udpipe): C++ with bindings; code **MPL 2.0**, pre-trained\n    models **CC BY-NC-SA** ([ÚFAL](https://ufal.mff.cuni.cz/udpipe/1)); models for 50+ languages.\n  - [Stanza](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2003.07082) (Stanford): Python/PyTorch, **Apache 2.0**, ~70\n    languages; model licenses follow source treebanks.\n  - [spaCy](https://explosion.ai/blog/ud-benchmarks-v3-2): Python/Cython, **MIT** code; trained\n    pipelines for ~25 languages, mostly permissive licensed.\n  - [Trankit](https://github.com/nlp-uoregon/trankit): transformer-based (XLM-R), **Apache 2.0**,\n    ~56 languages, ~90 pretrained pipelines; best UD accuracy of the four\n    ([performance docs](https://trankit.readthedocs.io/en/latest/performance.html)).\n- **Correctness vs annotation:** all four **annotate only** — they never reject input.\n  Grammaticality could at best be approximated by parse-score thresholds (unreliable).\n- **Rust:** none are Rust-native; UDPipe 1 is embeddable C++ (FFI feasible); ONNX export of\n  neural models is possible *(unverified for these specific tools)*. Output (CoNLL-U) is\n  Rust-friendly.\n- **Test corpora:** UD treebank test splits; CoNLL 2017/2018 shared-task data.\n- **Standout ideas:** language-agnostic single-model pipelines (Trankit's shared multilingual\n  encoder with per-language adapters) show that one engine can serve ~100 languages.\n\n### Apertium (rule-based MT) and lttoolbox\n\n- **What it does:** free/open-source rule-based shallow-transfer machine translation platform\n  ([apertium.org](https://apertium.org/), [wiki](https://wiki.apertium.org/wiki/Lttoolbox)).\n- **Formalism:** finite-state morphology ([lttoolbox](https://github.com/apertium/lttoolbox):\n  `lt-comp`/`lt-proc` over XML `.dix` dictionaries), CG-3 or HMM disambiguation, chunk-based\n  structural transfer rules.\n- **Coverage:** ~50 released translation pairs, dozens more in incubation; monolingual\n  morphological analyzers for far more languages *(pair count unverified; varies by release)*.\n- **Correctness vs annotation:** morphological analyzers **reject unknown/invalid word forms**\n  (a word either has an analysis or not) — i.e., word-level grammatical correctness; sentence\n  syntax is only shallowly checked (no full parse, so no full-sentence grammaticality).\n- **Data & licenses:** everything **GPL** ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apertium)).\n  Dictionaries are clean XML, easy to mine (lemma + paradigm + tags).\n- **Rust:** no official Rust port; lttoolbox is C++ (FFI possible). The `.dix` XML format is\n  trivially parseable from Rust.\n- **Test corpora:** per-pair regression tests and quality evaluations in each `apertium-XX-YY`\n  repo on [github.com/apertium](https://github.com/apertium).\n- **Standout ideas:** morphology as a finite-state transducer compiled from declarative paradigm\n  data — exactly the kind of data that can be re-expressed as links (lemma —paradigm→ form —tags→\n  features); pipeline-of-streams architecture.\n\n### LanguageTool\n\n- **What it does:** style and grammar checker for **31 languages**\n  ([languagetool.org/dev](https://languagetool.org/dev),\n  [GitHub](https://github.com/languagetool-org/languagetool)).\n- **Formalism:** ~thousands of declarative **XML error-pattern rules** (token/POS regex over a\n  tagged, chunked sentence) plus Java rules; no full parse — it detects *known error patterns*\n  rather than proving grammaticality.\n- **Correctness vs annotation:** **checks correctness negatively**: absence of triggered rules ≠\n  grammatical; presence of a triggered rule = specific, explainable error with suggested fix.\n  Complementary to precision grammars (which prove grammaticality positively but can't explain).\n- **Data & licenses:** **LGPL 2.1+** ([dev page](https://languagetool.org/dev)); rule XML files\n  ship with the source.\n- **Rust:** see nlprule below; also [`languagetool-rust`](https://crates.io/crates/languagetool-rust)\n  (HTTP client for the LT server).\n- **Test corpora:** each XML rule embeds `<example correction=...>` positive/negative example\n  sentences — thousands of built-in grammaticality/ungrammaticality test pairs per language.\n- **Standout ideas:** error rules with embedded test examples; per-language community-maintained\n  declarative rule files that a links engine could import directly.\n\n### nlprule (Rust port of LanguageTool rules)\n\n- **What it does:** [nlprule](https://github.com/bminixhofer/nlprule) re-implements\n  LanguageTool's rule engine and tagging/chunking/disambiguation pipeline in pure Rust.\n- **Coverage:** English, German, Spanish rule binaries (compiled from LanguageTool v5.2).\n- **Licenses:** code **MIT OR Apache-2.0**; the compiled `.bin` rule sets are derived from\n  LanguageTool and remain **LGPL 2.1** ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/nlprule/latest/nlprule/)).\n- **Status:** low maintenance activity since ~2021–2023; rules frozen at LT 5.2 *(activity level\n  unverified beyond crate metadata)*.\n- **Standout ideas:** proves LT's full rule semantics are portable to Rust with small binaries\n  and no JVM; its rule-compilation pipeline (`nlprule-build`) is a model for \"compile external\n  grammar data into a fast native format\".\n\n### HPSG / DELPH-IN (ERG, ACE, Grammar Matrix)\n\n- **What it does:** consortium building hand-engineered **precision grammars**\n  ([delph-in.github.io](https://delph-in.github.io/docs/home/Home/)). The\n  [English Resource Grammar](https://github.com/delph-in/erg) maps running English to normalized\n  logical forms; [ACE](https://delph-in.github.io/docs/tools/ToolsTop/) parses *and generates*\n  from the same grammar.\n- **Formalism:** **HPSG** (typed feature structures, unification) with **Minimal Recursion\n  Semantics** (MRS) output. The\n  [Grammar Matrix](https://delph-in.github.io/docs/howto/DelphinTutorial_Grammars/) is a\n  questionnaire-driven starter kit that emits a working HPSG grammar for a new language.\n- **Coverage:** ERG (English) is broad-coverage; other mature grammars: Jacy (Japanese), GG\n  (German), Zhong (Chinese), SRG (Spanish), etc.; Matrix-derived grammars for many small\n  languages. Far from top-10 coverage at ERG quality.\n- **Correctness vs annotation:** **strict grammaticality checking** — a precision grammar rejects\n  ungrammatical input (ERG additionally has optional \"mal-rules\" for robust parsing of errors,\n  used in grammar-coaching research, e.g.\n  [GAUSS](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.18340)).\n- **Data & licenses:** open-source; ERG under an MIT-style license *(exact license text\n  unverified)*; tools open source per\n  [DELPH-IN overview](https://delph-in.github.io/docs/home/Home/).\n- **Rust:** none; ACE is C (FFI feasible); `pydelphin` is the Python tooling.\n- **Test corpora:** `[incr tsdb()]` test-suite profiles and the Redwoods treebank distributed\n  with ERG releases ([ERG docs](https://delph-in.github.io/docs/erg/ErgTop/)).\n- **Standout ideas:** \"mal-rules\" (explicitly modeled error rules) give *explainable*\n  ungrammaticality; bidirectional parse/generate from one declarative grammar; Grammar Matrix\n  shows grammars can be generated from typological feature choices.\n\n### LFG / XLE (ParGram)\n\n- **What it does:** [XLE](https://ling.sprachwiss.uni-konstanz.de/pages/xle/) parses/generates\n  Lexical-Functional Grammars; basis of the **ParGram** parallel-grammar consortium (grammars for\n  English, French, German, Norwegian, Japanese, Urdu, Turkish, Polish, Welsh, Wolof, …).\n- **Formalism:** **LFG** — parallel c-structure (phrase structure) and f-structure (functional,\n  attribute-value) representations; ParGram standardizes f-structure features across languages.\n- **Correctness vs annotation:** precision grammars — **reject ungrammatical input**; XLE has\n  robustness/fragment modes and OT-marks for graded grammaticality.\n- **Licenses:** XLE is **proprietary (PARC copyright), free only by research license** — a\n  practical dead end for open-source reuse. Open alternatives exist but are immature\n  (e.g. [Free Linguistic Environment](https://github.com/dcavar/fle)).\n- **Rust:** none.\n- **Test corpora:** ParGram test suites; INESS treebanks (Norwegian infrastructure)\n  *(availability details unverified)*.\n- **Standout ideas:** ParGram's *parallel f-structures* — same functional attribute space across\n  languages with language-specific phrase structure — is a strong precedent for \"shared abstract\n  layer, per-language surface layer\".\n\n### Constraint Grammar (VISL CG-3)\n\n- **What it does:** [CG-3](https://edu.visl.dk/cg3/single/) applies hand-written contextual\n  REMOVE/SELECT/ADD rules to disambiguate morphological readings and add syntactic tags.\n- **Formalism:** Constraint Grammar (reductionist, rule-based tagging over ambiguous FST output).\n- **Coverage:** grammars for **30+ languages**\n  ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constraint_grammar)); core of\n  [GiellaLT](https://giellalt.uit.no/tools/cg3-usage.html) infrastructure for Sámi and other\n  minority languages; also used inside Apertium pipelines.\n- **Correctness vs annotation:** primarily disambiguation/annotation, but GiellaLT's **Divvun\n  grammar checkers** are built from CG rules that detect real grammatical errors — CG is a proven\n  substrate for production grammar checking of morphologically rich languages.\n- **Licenses:** CG-3 is **GPL** ([UiO](https://www.uio.no/english/services/it/research/sensitive-data/help/hpc/software/VISL%20CG-3.html));\n  GiellaLT grammars are open source.\n- **Rust:** none; CG-3 is C++ (`cg3` CLI / library, FFI feasible).\n- **Test corpora:** GiellaLT per-language regression test suites (yaml tests in `lang-*` repos).\n- **Standout ideas:** contextual constraint rules are naturally expressible as link patterns\n  (\"remove reading X if a link to a finite verb exists to the left\"); proven on low-resource,\n  morphology-heavy languages.\n\n### UniMorph\n\n- **What it does:** universal schema + datasets for inflectional morphology\n  ([unimorph.github.io](https://unimorph.github.io/)): triples *(lemma, inflected form, feature\n  bundle)*.\n- **Formalism:** the UniMorph feature schema (universal inventory of morphological features).\n- **Coverage:** **169+ languages** annotated ([UniMorph 4.0](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.03608)).\n- **Correctness vs annotation:** data, not a checker — but the tables directly support\n  **word-form validation** (is this form a valid inflection of this lemma with these features?).\n- **Licenses:** open source; per-language repos mostly **CC BY-SA 3.0** (much data derives from\n  Wiktionary) *(per-repo license must be checked; unverified globally)*.\n- **Rust:** plain TSV — trivially loadable; no dedicated crate needed.\n- **Test corpora:** SIGMORPHON shared-task splits (e.g.\n  [2022InflectionST](https://github.com/sigmorphon/2022InflectionST)).\n- **Standout ideas:** a universal morphological feature vocabulary aligned with UD features —\n  the natural feature alphabet for morphology links in a links network.\n\n---\n\n## Shared concept spaces and interlinguas\n\n### WordNet, Open English WordNet, Open Multilingual Wordnet (OMW) + CILI\n\n- **What it does:** Princeton WordNet groups words into **synsets** (concepts) linked by\n  hypernymy etc.; [OMW](https://omwn.org/) federates 40+ open wordnets;\n  [CILI](https://github.com/globalwordnet/cili) (Collaborative Interlingual Index) assigns a\n  **stable language-independent ILI identifier to every concept**, so wordnets in different\n  languages link to the same ILI only when the concept matches\n  ([CILI paper](https://aclanthology.org/2016.gwc-1.9/)).\n- **Coverage:** OMW: 40+ languages with open licenses; Open English WordNet\n  ([globalwordnet/english-wordnet](https://github.com/globalwordnet/english-wordnet), CC BY 4.0)\n  is the maintained English hub; CILI itself is CC BY.\n- **Exact-match semantics:** CILI's policy is essentially issue #47's rule: a new concept gets a\n  **new ILI id** unless it exactly matches an existing one; ILI definitions are frozen to prevent\n  drift.\n- **Data & licenses:** open (CC BY / wordnet licenses); machine-readable **WN-LMF XML** and RDF\n  ([Global WordNet formats](https://globalwordnet.github.io/schemas/)); Python\n  [`wn`](https://github.com/goodmami/wn) library implements interlingual queries via ILI.\n- **Rust:** WN-LMF is plain XML; small wordnet crates exist but none is canonical *(unverified)*.\n- **Test corpora:** SemCor and wordnet gloss corpora (English); per-wordnet validation in OMW.\n- **Standout ideas:** the **ILI = concept-as-link-id** model; \"reuse only on exact match,\n  otherwise mint a new id\" is institutionalized here. The single most directly relevant design.\n\n### BabelNet\n\n- **What it does:** merges WordNet, Wikipedia, Wikidata, Wiktionary etc. into multilingual\n  synsets ([babelnet.org/about](https://babelnet.org/about)).\n- **Coverage:** v5.3: **600 languages, ~23M synsets, ~1.7B senses**\n  ([statistics](https://babelnet.org/statistics)).\n- **Exact match:** synsets merge senses across resources — merging is automatic and noisy, the\n  *opposite* of strict exact-match minting.\n- **Licenses:** **CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 + custom non-commercial research license**, API-key gated\n  ([license](https://babelnet.org/license)) — **not redistributable / not usable** in an\n  open-source MIT-style project. Treat as inspiration only.\n- **Rust:** HTTP API only.\n- **Standout ideas:** scale of automatic sense linking; Babel synset ids as cross-resource glue.\n\n### ConceptNet\n\n- **What it does:** commonsense knowledge graph of words/phrases\n  ([conceptnet.io](https://conceptnet.io/)); edges like `/c/en/dog —IsA→ /c/en/animal`.\n- **Coverage:** **304 languages** (deep coverage in ~10); ~34M assertions in 5.7\n  ([release post](http://blog.conceptnet.io/posts/2019/conceptnet-57-released/)).\n- **Exact match:** nodes are **surface terms, not disambiguated senses** — `/c/en/bank` is one\n  node for all meanings. Fails issue #47's exact-match requirement at the concept level.\n- **Licenses:** **CC BY-SA 4.0**, bulk TSV download\n  ([downloads](https://github.com/commonsense/conceptnet5/wiki/Downloads)) — open and usable\n  (share-alike applies to derived data).\n- **Rust:** plain TSV; no canonical crate.\n- **Standout ideas:** URI scheme for multilingual terms; relation vocabulary usable as link\n  types; cross-lingual `SynonymOf`/`TranslationOf` edges as *candidate* (not exact) alignments.\n\n### Wikidata lexemes\n\n- **What it does:** Wikidata's lexicographical layer\n  ([Lexicographical data](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Lexicographical_data)): Lexeme\n  (L-id) → Forms (inflections with features) and Senses; a Sense can link via \"item for this\n  sense\" (P5137) to a Wikidata **Q-item**, which is the language-independent concept.\n- **Coverage:** **1.3M+ lexemes** across hundreds of languages\n  ([stats](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Lexicographical_data/Statistics/Count_of_lexemes,_forms,_and_senses_by_language));\n  uneven per language.\n- **Exact match:** Q-items are minted per distinct concept with notability rules; sense→Q-item\n  links are explicit editorial assertions — a workable exact-match discipline, community-governed.\n- **Licenses:** **CC0 (public domain)** for all lexeme/item data\n  ([licensing](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Licensing)) — the most permissive concept\n  space available, safe for any downstream license.\n- **Rust:** JSON dumps + SPARQL; community crates for Wikidata JSON exist (e.g. `wikidata` on\n  crates.io) *(crate quality unverified)*.\n- **Test corpora:** none as such; data is the resource.\n- **Standout ideas:** separation **Lexeme (language-bound) vs Q-item (language-free concept)**\n  with an explicit link between them = precisely the two-layer architecture issue #47 needs;\n  Forms with feature bundles double as morphological validation data.\n\n### Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR)\n\n- **What it does:** sentence-level semantic graphs (PENMAN notation) abstracting away syntax\n  ([amr.isi.edu](https://amr.isi.edu/)); concepts mostly PropBank framesets.\n- **Coverage:** English-centric; AMR 3.0 sembank = **59,255 sentences**, distributed by **LDC\n  under fee/membership license** ([LDC2020T02](https://catalog.ldc.upenn.edu/LDC2020T02)) —\n  annotation *guidelines* are public, the corpus is not freely redistributable.\n- **Exact match:** AMR explicitly does **not** aim at interlingual identity (English-biased\n  concept inventory).\n- **Rust:** PENMAN format is easy to parse; no canonical crate.\n- **Standout ideas:** graphs (re-entrancy for coreference) rather than trees; concept+role\n  normalization shows what a \"semantic layer above grammar\" looks like — out of scope for #47's\n  no-semantics rule but relevant later.\n\n### Uniform Meaning Representation (UMR)\n\n- **What it does:** AMR's multilingual, document-level successor\n  ([umr4nlp.github.io](https://umr4nlp.github.io/web/)); adds aspect, scope, modality,\n  inter-sentential coreference; designed for low-resource languages.\n- **Coverage:** UMR v2.0: **8 languages** (English, Chinese, Czech, Latin, Arapaho, Kukama,\n  Navajo, Sanapaná), **210k+ sentence-level UMRs**\n  ([data page](https://umr4nlp.github.io/web/data.html),\n  [infrastructure paper](https://openreview.net/forum?id=Vb4547RFqJ)).\n- **Licenses:** released openly (LINDAT/GitHub; CC-style) *(exact license per release\n  unverified)* — unlike AMR's LDC gating.\n- **Standout ideas:** lattice-based feature values (languages pick granularity along shared\n  lattices) — a principled way to share a concept/feature space *without* forcing false exact\n  matches; directly relevant to \"reuse only on exact match\".\n\n### UNL (Universal Networking Language)\n\n- **What it does:** 1996 UNU initiative: sentences as hypergraphs of **Universal Words** (UWs)\n  linked by ~40 semantic relations and attributes\n  ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Networking_Language),\n  [UNL archive](https://www.unlarchive.org/wiki/Introduction_to_UNL)).\n- **Status:** effectively **defunct** — UNDL Foundation dissolved (project wind-down reported\n  2015–2024; [archive](http://www.unlweb.net/)); resources scattered, licenses unclear. Historical\n  prior art only.\n- **Exact match:** UWs are English headwords + constraint lists (`drink(icl>liquor)`) — concepts\n  are *named*, human-readable, and disambiguated by typed constraints rather than opaque ids.\n- **Standout ideas:** self-describing concept identifiers (headword + constraints) and the\n  cautionary tale: a centrally-managed closed interlingua dies with its institution. Favor\n  open, community-minted ids (CILI/Wikidata) instead.\n\n### Abstract Wikipedia / Wikifunctions\n\n- **What it does:** Wikimedia project to store encyclopedic content as language-independent\n  **abstract content** (constructors) rendered into natural languages by **Wikifunctions**\n  renderer functions using **Wikidata lexemes**\n  ([Abstract Wikipedia](https://meta.wikimedia.org/wiki/Abstract_Wikipedia),\n  [NLG architecture proposal](https://meta.wikimedia.org/wiki/Abstract_Wikipedia/Natural_language_generation_system_architecture_proposal)).\n- **Status (2026-06):** active; 2025 \"fragment experiments\" generate sentence fragments in\n  multiple languages from lexemes\n  ([2025 fragment experiments](https://www.wikifunctions.org/wiki/Wikifunctions:Abstract_Wikipedia/2025_fragment_experiments));\n  soft launch targeted 2026 ([status updates](https://www.wikifunctions.org/wiki/Wikifunctions:Status_updates)).\n- **Licenses:** Wikifunctions code/content under free licenses (Apache-2/CC); data CC0 via\n  Wikidata.\n- **Standout ideas:** the **closest living competitor** to issue #47's end goal: abstract\n  content + per-language renderer functions + CC0 lexeme layer. Its NLG architecture debate\n  (template renderers vs GF-style grammars, Ninai/Udiron tree toolkit) is required reading.\n  Currently generation-only — it does not *parse* natural language, which leaves #47's parsing\n  niche open.\n\n### FrameNet\n\n- **What it does:** lexicon of **semantic frames** (events/situations with roles) and\n  frame-annotated sentences ([framenet.icsi.berkeley.edu](https://framenet.icsi.berkeley.edu/framenet_data)).\n- **Coverage:** English release 1.7: **~1,221 frames, ~13.6k lexical units**\n  ([FrameNet at 25](http://sites.la.utexas.edu/hcb/files/2025/05/Boas-et-al-2025-FrameNet.pdf));\n  independent framenets exist for Swedish, Japanese, Brazilian Portuguese, German, etc. (not one\n  shared id space).\n- **Licenses:** data freely downloadable; release 1.7 under CC BY 4.0 *(license version\n  unverified — confirm on download form)*.\n- **Standout ideas:** frames as interlingual-ish *event concepts* with typed roles; Multilingual\n  FrameNet alignment shows frames only partially match across languages — evidence for strict\n  exact-match policies.\n\n### PropBank\n\n- **What it does:** verb sense inventory (\"rolesets\", e.g. `run.01`) with numbered arguments;\n  the concept vocabulary underlying AMR/UMR\n  ([propbank.github.io](https://propbank.github.io/)).\n- **Coverage:** English frames v3.4 (~11k rolesets *(count unverified)*); Universal Proposition\n  Banks project transfer to ~20 languages\n  ([UP-1.0](https://github.com/UniversalPropositions/UP-1.0)).\n- **Licenses:** frame files **CC BY-SA 4.0**\n  ([propbank-frames](https://github.com/propbank/propbank-frames)); annotations are pointers —\n  full text requires LDC corpora (OntoNotes).\n- **Standout ideas:** stable, versioned, machine-readable XML sense ids that other projects\n  (AMR, UMR) reuse — a working example of a shared concept id registry with governance.\n\n---\n\n## Recommended approach signals\n\nFor a Rust links-network engine needing (1) grammatical-correctness parsing of the top-10\nlanguages and (2) an exact-match shared concept space:\n\n### Grammatical-correctness parsing\n\n1. **GF + RGL is the only off-the-shelf system that does exactly what issue #47 asks** —\n   parse-or-reject grammaticality with *no* semantic checks, for 40+ languages including the\n   top 10, under LGPL/BSD, with a compiled grammar format (PGF/JSON) already consumable from Rust\n   via [`gf-core`](https://crates.io/crates/gf-core). The abstract/concrete split maps naturally\n   onto a links network (abstract tree nodes = shared links; linearizations = per-language\n   links). Main risks: `gf-core` is young (consider implementing a native PMCFG/PGF reader on\n   links), and RGL coverage is \"core grammar\", not robust open-text parsing.\n2. **Layer the morphology from open FST/table data**: Apertium `.dix` (GPL — keep as optional\n   data), UniMorph TSV (CC BY-SA), and **Wikidata lexeme Forms (CC0)** give word-level\n   correctness (valid form ⇔ exists with features) without any C++ dependency. CC0 lexemes are\n   the safest default.\n3. **Use UD as the naming standard, not the checker**: adopt UPOS/UFeats/UD relations as the\n   link-type vocabulary so every UD treebank (179 languages) becomes import/test data, and UD\n   test splits become regression corpora — while grammaticality itself is decided by the\n   GF-style generative layer. Rust crates `rs-conllu`/`conllu` already read the format.\n4. **Borrow negative-evidence rules**: LanguageTool XML rules (LGPL) with their embedded\n   example sentences provide thousands of ready-made pass/fail test cases per language; nlprule\n   proves the engine fits in Rust. DELPH-IN's \"mal-rules\" pattern (explicit error rules alongside\n   the grammar) is the right mechanism for *explaining* why a parse fails.\n5. **Avoid as cores**: XLE (proprietary), neural UD parsers (annotate-only, Python/C++ stacks,\n   some NC-licensed models) — usable as offline preprocessing/bootstrapping tools only.\n\n### Exact-match shared concept space\n\n1. **Adopt the two-layer Wikidata model**: language-bound *lexeme* (lemma + forms + features)\n   linked to a language-free *concept id*. Wikidata lexemes + Q-items are **CC0**, multilingual,\n   and continuously growing — the only major concept space with zero licensing friction.\n2. **Use CILI as the minting discipline and secondary id space**: Open English WordNet (CC BY)\n   + OMW wordnets keyed by **ILI ids** implement \"reuse only on exact match, else mint a new id\"\n   today; WN-LMF XML is easy to load in Rust. Store ILI and Q-ids as aliases of one links-node.\n3. **PropBank frames (CC BY-SA) and FrameNet frames** are good optional registries for\n   *event/predicate* concepts when verbs need argument-structure identity, but keep them out of\n   the grammaticality layer (#47 forbids semantic checks).\n4. **Reject BabelNet** (non-commercial, API-gated) and **ConceptNet as a concept layer**\n   (surface words, not senses; CC BY-SA contamination risk) — ConceptNet is acceptable only as\n   candidate-alignment evidence. **UNL** is a cautionary tale: closed governance killed it.\n5. **Watch Abstract Wikipedia/Wikifunctions** (soft launch ~2026): same architecture\n   (abstract content + lexemes + renderers), CC0-adjacent, but generation-only — meta-language's\n   differentiator is *bidirectional* parse/generate over a lossless links substrate, with\n   GF-style abstract syntax for grammar and Wikidata/CILI ids for the exact-match concept space.\n\n### Licensing summary table\n\n| Resource | License | Safe for permissive Rust crate? |\n|---|---|---|\n| GF RGL / runtime | LGPL + BSD | Yes (link as data/runtime; check per-module) |\n| `gf-core` crate | MIT/Apache *(verify)* | Yes |\n| UD treebanks | mixed CC BY-SA / CC BY-NC-SA | Per-treebank; tests only is safest |\n| LanguageTool rules / nlprule bins | LGPL 2.1 | As external data files, yes |\n| Apertium data | GPL | Only as optional external data |\n| UniMorph | mostly CC BY-SA 3.0 | Yes, with attribution/share-alike on data |\n| ERG / DELPH-IN | MIT-style *(verify)* | Yes |\n| XLE | proprietary | No |\n| Wikidata (lexemes + items) | **CC0** | Yes — preferred |\n| OEWN / OMW / CILI | CC BY (mostly) | Yes |\n| PropBank frames | CC BY-SA 4.0 | Yes (share-alike on data) |\n| FrameNet 1.7 | CC BY *(verify version)* | Likely yes |\n| ConceptNet | CC BY-SA 4.0 | Data layer only, share-alike |\n| BabelNet | CC BY-NC-SA + custom | **No** |\n| AMR 3.0 corpus | LDC | No (guidelines only) |\n| UMR corpora | open *(verify per release)* | Likely yes |\n"

[2026-06-10T14:23:17.871Z] [INFO]           "content": "# Competitor Case Study: Source-Code Syntax Tooling\n\nResearch date: **2026-06-10**. Scope: tools that parse, query, and transform source code syntax — the\nclosest competitors to meta-language's lossless links network with CST/AST/semantic projections,\n`LinkQuery`, and `find()`/`replace()` transforms.\n\nMethod: every repository below was inspected via the GitHub API on 2026-06-10 (license, activity,\ndirectory layout of the test corpus); doc claims were checked against the projects' official\ndocumentation. Facts that could not be verified are marked **(unverified)**.\n\nLegend for each section: (a) what it is / primary languages, (b) read-only vs mutable syntax model,\n(c) lossless / trivia preservation, (d) query language, (e) transform/codemod support,\n(f) multi-language breadth, (g) extensibility, (h) license, (i) test-suite location and shape,\n(j) standout feature meta-language lacks.\n\n---\n\n## tree-sitter\n\n- (a) Incremental parsing system for programming tools, written in Rust/C (core) with grammars\n  compiled from JS DSL to C. Repo: <https://github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter> (25.7k stars, active\n  as of 2026-06-10).\n- (b) **Read-only** CST. Trees are immutable; \"editing\" means telling the parser about source edits\n  and re-parsing incrementally — there is no tree mutation API.\n- (c) Lossless in the sense that every byte is covered by the tree (named + anonymous nodes, `extra`\n  nodes for comments/whitespace handled by grammar), with `ERROR`/`MISSING` recovery nodes. The tree\n  stores spans into the original text rather than owning text.\n- (d) **Tree-sitter query language**: S-expression patterns with field names (`left:`), negated\n  fields (`!field`), wildcards (`_`/`(_)`), quantifiers, anchors, captures (`@name`), predicates\n  (`#eq?`, `#match?`), and `(ERROR)`/`(MISSING)` matching. Docs:\n  <https://tree-sitter.github.io/tree-sitter/using-parsers/queries/1-syntax.html>.\n- (e) No transform support — queries are match-only; rewriting is left to consumers (ast-grep,\n  difftastic, editors).\n- (f) Hundreds of community grammars (one repo per language under the `tree-sitter` org and beyond).\n- (g) Extensible by writing a new grammar (`grammar.js` + optional external C scanner for\n  context-sensitive lexing).\n- (h) MIT.\n- (i) Tests: core runtime tests in `test/fixtures/` (subdirs `error_corpus/`, `template_corpus/`,\n  `grammars/`, `test_grammars/`, `fixtures.json`) — e.g. `test/fixtures/error_corpus/javascript_errors.txt`.\n  Each grammar repo has the canonical **corpus format**: `test/corpus/*.txt` files where each case is\n  `=== name ===`, source code, `---`, then the expected S-expression tree (see\n  <https://github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter-javascript/tree/master/test/corpus> —\n  `destructuring.txt`, `expressions.txt`, `semicolon_insertion.txt`, … — and the format docs at\n  <https://tree-sitter.github.io/tree-sitter/creating-parsers/5-writing-tests.html>). Grammar repos\n  also carry `test/highlight/` and `test/tags/` assertion files.\n- (j) **Incremental re-parsing** after edits, error-recovery corpora, and the de-facto-standard\n  corpus test format (meta-language already mimics the query syntax; the corpus format and\n  incremental reparse are the gaps).\n\n## ast-grep\n\n- (a) CLI for structural search, lint, and rewriting built on tree-sitter, written in Rust. Repo:\n  <https://github.com/ast-grep/ast-grep> (14.4k stars, active).\n- (b) Read-only tree-sitter CSTs; edits are produced as text replacements computed from matches, not\n  by mutating the tree.\n- (c) Inherits tree-sitter's full-coverage CST; rewrites splice replacement text into original\n  source, preserving untouched bytes.\n- (d) Two query surfaces: **pattern code** (write the code you want to match, with `$META` /\n  `$$$MULTI` metavariables) and a **YAML rule language** composing atomic rules (`pattern`, `kind`,\n  `regex`), relational rules (`inside`, `has`, `precedes`, `follows`), and composite rules\n  (`all`/`any`/`not`/`matches`), plus reusable `utils`. Docs: <https://ast-grep.github.io/>.\n- (e) Yes: `fix:` rewrites in rules, `rewriters` for nested transformations, interactive `ast-grep\n  scan --interactive` codemod mode; also Node/Python APIs (`@ast-grep/napi`, `pyo3` crates).\n- (f) Any language with a tree-sitter grammar; ~25 built in, more via dynamic libraries.\n- (g) Custom languages via dynamically loaded tree-sitter parsers (`crates/dynamic`,\n  `fixtures/json-linux.so` in-repo); language bindings via napi/pyo3/wasm crates.\n- (h) MIT.\n- (i) Tests: Rust unit tests inline in `crates/core`, `crates/config`, `crates/cli/src` (note\n  `crates/cli/src/verify/` implements the user-facing test framework). The **user-level rule-test\n  format** is the portable asset: a `rule-tests/` dir with `<rule>-test.yml` files containing\n  `valid:` / `invalid:` code lists plus `__snapshots__/` of expected diagnostics, driven by\n  `ast-grep test` (<https://ast-grep.github.io/guide/test-rule.html>).\n- (j) **Composable YAML rule algebra** (relational + boolean rule composition with named utility\n  rules) and a built-in **rule snapshot-testing harness** with valid/invalid/noisy/missing\n  classification.\n\n## Semgrep (syntax-pattern subset)\n\n- (a) Lightweight static-analysis engine; patterns look like the target language's source code.\n  OCaml core + Python CLI. Repo: <https://github.com/semgrep/semgrep> (15.4k stars, active).\n- (b) Read-only AST (per-language parsers normalized into a generic AST in OCaml).\n- (c) Not lossless — it works on a normalized AST; autofix is span-based text replacement on\n  original source rather than tree printing.\n- (d) Pattern syntax: `$METAVARIABLES`, `...` ellipsis (statements/args), deep-expression\n  `<... e ...>`, typed metavariables, `pattern-either`/`patterns`/`pattern-not`/`pattern-inside`\n  composition in YAML rules, plus `metavariable-regex`/`-comparison`.
